title: Who and Which: Relative Clauses on the High Plateau

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know relative clauses with *que* and *quien* from B1 Unit 5. A relative clause adds information about a noun without starting a new sentence: *la planta que crece en el agua*. *Que* works for things, animals and people. *Quien* is only for people, and it is most useful after a preposition: *la guía con quien viajamos*. Here you use them to describe the high plateau and Lake Titicaca.

sections.title: Que and quien at work
rows: El lago Titicaca, que está entre Bolivia y Perú, es muy alto.
Lake Titicaca, which is between Bolivia and Peru, is very high. (*que* + a comma: extra information)
La totora es una planta que crece en el agua.
Totora is a plant that grows in the water. (*que* says which plant)
Los aymaras que viven junto al lago cultivan papa.
The Aymara people who live next to the lake grow potatoes. (*que* for people)
La guía con quien viajamos conoce bien la isla.
The guide we travelled with knows the island well. (*quien* after a preposition)

items.spanish: Las llamas pastan en los bofedales, que son humedales de altura.
items.english: Llamas graze in the bofedales, which are high wetlands.

items.spanish: Las comunidades que viven junto al lago cultivan papa y quinua.
items.english: The communities that live next to the lake grow potatoes and quinoa.

items.spanish: La Isla del Sol, que se visita en barco, tiene ruinas de piedra.
items.english: The Island of the Sun, which you visit by boat, has stone ruins.

sections.content: Never leave *que* out, as English sometimes does: *the plants we saw* is *las plantas que vimos*. The verb after *que* agrees with the noun before it: *los aymaras que viven*, not *que vive*.
